newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Sheep join Serbian opposition protest.
newsitem.headline: Sheep join Serbian opposition protest.

text.p: Sheep took to the streets on Sunday with Serbian anti-government protesters in the opposition's latest bid to ridicule supporters of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

The four animals, brought to the rally in Belgrade by Ljubinko Cvetkovic, a farmer from central Serbia, bore signs saying "RTS (Serbian television) is our pen", "The world is against us", and "We are Slobo's (Milosevic), Slobo is ours".

Vuk Draskovic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) coalition which has mounted the protests to force Milosevic to recognise its victories in November 17 elections, told the rally and an earlier news conference that opening tightly-controlled state media to the opposition was one of Zajedno's main demands.

"Our condition of all conditions for any dialogue is the recognition of all November 17 election results," Draskovic said at the demonstration by an estimated 20,000 people in Belgrade's central Republic Square.
"After the recognition of those results, we shall begin dialogue at once -- under one single condition -- that this dialogue is broadcast on state TV and that all state media report about it.
"We do not want isolation for our homeland, we want economic and all-round social revival," Draskovic said.

Draskovic made a similar point after opposition leaders met visiting Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos who flew in for separate talks with Milosevic, the Zajedno coalition and Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic.

"We are ready for dialogue and we are ready to stop the demonstrations....(but) that dialogue must be expressed in the media -- state media -- in a free and open way," Draskovic said at a joint news conference with Pangalos.

Vesna Pesic of the Serbian Civic Alliance (GSS), a member of the Zajedno leadership troika, said at the rally that Pangalos had told Milosevic Greece supported a report of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which found the elections were fair.

"After Mr Pangalos told Milosevic that Greece would support the OSCE report, our Mr Dictator said that for him that question had been resolved in the institutions of our system and the 'independent' judiciary," Pesic said.
"But we have no rights here at all. Not even our elementary voting rights are respected here."
The sheep stayed with the demonstrators as they walked through central Belgrade and were stopped by a police cordon set up on Jula Street.

For more than two weeks there has been no violence during the demonstrations. Police make a show of maintaining a cordon to block the marchers but the demonstrators can easily walk around the police lines and spend much of their time talking with the police and even posing with them for pictures.
